berthe-morisot.rationale: Morisot puts her husband at the far left of her Cowes portrait. Following his gaze takes the viewer through a pane of glass to the garden and waterfront. In the Bougival paintings, foliage appears to enter the room. Across these pictures she changes what counts as the subject of a portrait and where the viewer stands in relation to it.

sources.label: Tokyo Fuji Art Museum · On the Terrace

sources.label: Musée d’Orsay · Windows and thresholds
sources.evidence: This section of the exhibition distinguishes the use of windows in her Bougival paintings from a domestic storyline. Interior and exterior merge, leaving the viewer to work out where the space changes.

sources.label: Musée d’Orsay · The Cradle
sources.evidence: The linked arms of mother and baby and the mother’s gaze organize the scene around the sleeping child.

sections.communicates.examples: In The Cradle, a woman watches a sleeping infant through a veil of white fabric. The bend of her arm echoes the baby’s arm, connecting them across the space between their faces.
Summer’s Day seats two women in an open boat. Morisot lets brisk marks for light and water remain visible around them, so the still figures share the movement of the lake.

In Eugène Manet on the Isle of Wight (1875), Morisot placed her husband at the left of a hotel window in Cowes. The same pane frames the garden and waterfront, so the viewer can look beyond the sitter and out with him.
Hanging the Laundry out to Dry sets people doing the wash within a broad, open landscape. The line of pale fabric gives the eye a way across the canvas and gives everyday work a place in the view.

fanny-blankers-koen.rationale: At her Amsterdam homecoming, Blankers-Koen described the fuss over her four golds in terms of the races she had run. In 2001 a reporter compared her prize bicycle with a later champion’s sponsorship deal. She answered by recalling how long the bicycle lasted and what it meant to race again after the war. Each answer changed the measure of the achievement the question had supplied.
fanny-blankers-koen.scope: How Blankers-Koen answered public questions about her Olympic career

sources.label: Duncan Mackay · Interview with Blankers-Koen, recalled in The Irish Times
sources.evidence: Mackay recounts his 2001 question comparing the bicycle Amsterdam gave her with a later sprinter’s endorsement. Blankers-Koen answered with the years the bicycle served her and what competing after the war meant to her.

sources.label: Australian Broadcasting Corporation · Guy Ryan remembers interviewing Blankers-Koen
sources.evidence: Ryan recalls his own one-on-one interview in the Netherlands in 1948. He describes her modest public manner and separately gives his own judgment of her effect on acceptance of women in elite athletics.

sources.label: State Library of Western Australia · signed 1949 tour programme
sources.evidence: The programme documents her Australian appearance in women’s athletics. It does not record a specific request she made to an organizer on another athlete’s behalf.

sources.label: World Athletics · Fanny Blankers-Koen’s London events
sources.evidence: Under the cap of three individual events plus the relay, she competed in the 100 metres, 200 metres, 80 metres hurdles and the relay. She won all four.

sources.label: Guus van Holland · NRC Handelsblad roundtable with Blankers-Koen, 2 January 1999
sources.evidence: Asked what she earned, Blankers-Koen recalled having to surrender a pair of silver candlesticks. She acknowledged how much more modern athletes earned, then said the rivalry she saw in their sport made their pay less enviable to her.

sections.communicates.examples: At the 1948 London Olympics, Olympic rules limited athletes to three individual events plus a relay, so Blankers-Koen entered the 100m, 200m and 80m hurdles and the 4x100m relay, opting not to contest the high jump or long jump even though she was the world-record holder in both. She ran 11 races in eight days in London and won them all.

After winning four events in London in 1948, Blankers-Koen rode through Amsterdam in a public parade. When asked about the excitement surrounding her, she described the achievement simply as winning some footraces.

In a 2001 interview, Duncan Mackay contrasted the bicycle Amsterdam had given Blankers-Koen with a later champion’s sponsorship. Blankers-Koen recalled the years the bicycle lasted and how wartime disruption had once made competing again seem uncertain.
Competing under the name Koen at Berlin in 1936, she tied for sixth in the high jump and finished fifth with the Netherlands in the 4 × 100 metres relay.

previous_copy.sections.identity: The woman who won by choosing her lanes: a Dutch sprinter who set twelve official world records but made her name by narrowing four Olympic events down to the ones she could carry.
previous_copy.sections.pattern.1: The 1948 Games are the clearest public evidence of how she worked. Olympic rules allowed three individual events plus a relay, and she picked the 100m, 200m and 80m hurdles, leaving out the high jump and long jump even though she held world records in both. She then ran eleven races in eight days and won all of them, the relay included. Whatever one makes of her privately, the public choice was to trade optional glory for a load she could carry.
previous_copy.sections.communicates.text.0: Her public communication is largely the communication of decisions rather than speeches. The documented record speaks through event entries, withdrawals, team sheets and a handful of recalled conversations. When she does speak in the sources, it is in short, concrete anecdotes — an autograph, a meeting, a name she did not have to explain.
previous_copy.sections.communicates.text.1: That makes her legible to a reader in a specific way: you learn what she values from what she declines. Choosing three events over five when she held world records in the omitted ones is a form of saying no in public. A partner looking for a parallel should look less at what she says about herself and more at which commitments she keeps and which she drops without drama.

World Athletics profiles and championship media sheets carry her competitive marks and a few biographical notes — her son Zion's birth in 2017, her book — while her own published statements, such as the 2019 World Athletics Awards interview, centre on competition and craft. The pattern is a public figure who shares the work and the stated lessons, and leaves the rest unperformed.

This is a communication style that asks the audience to read the work first and the words second.

toussaint-louverture.rationale: In 1797 Louverture challenged a French legislator’s attack on abolition and warned the French Directory that restoring slavery would meet resistance. In 1800 he publicly accused French commissioner Roume of sowing discord and ordered him confined. These were distinct disputes with authorities on his own side. The second also shows the coercive power Louverture could exercise.

sections.communicates.examples: In 1801 Toussaint Louverture was named governor for life of Saint-Domingue under the colony's new constitution, which entrusted him with its direction for the remainder of his life in recognition of his services during the revolution.

In May 1794 Louverture explained to French general Étienne Laveaux why he had broken with Spain. He said Spain had offered freedom to those who fought for the Crown, but that he had come to fear a return to slavery.

On 12 October 1800, Louverture ordered managers, overseers and cultivators who failed in their assigned plantation duties to face arrest and military-style punishment. The same regulation required cultivators who had entered domestic service to return to their plantations.

In a signed letter to Charles Vincent in October 1797, Louverture challenged a French parliamentarian’s arguments against abolition in Saint-Domingue. The surviving letter records the objection of a general then serving under French authority.

matches.why: In 1797 Louverture challenged a French legislator’s attack on abolition and warned the French Directory that restoring slavery would meet resistance. In 1800 he publicly accused French commissioner Roume of sowing discord and ordered him confined. These were distinct disputes with authorities on his own side. The second also shows the coercive power Louverture could exercise.

sections.map.cousin.tell: Advocate fits his appeals for formerly enslaved people’s freedom. His order confining Roume records a rupture inside the French administration. On the plantations Louverture himself ordered military-style punishment and compelled workers to return, a limit on the freedoms he defended.

patch.sections.pattern.0: France’s National Convention decreed abolition on 4 February 1794. In May, Louverture wrote to General Laveaux explaining why he had broken with Spain. He said he feared a return to slavery. The choice marked a public disagreement with allies he had fought beside. In everyday terms, it is the moment a person tells their own side where they differ and stands by the reason, even when the timing is awkward. That is a stance about a principle, not a template for how to treat a partner.
patch.sections.pattern.2: Louverture’s 12 October 1800 regulation imposed military-style discipline on plantation labor. It required cultivators who had entered domestic service to return to their plantations. The rules tied compliance to consequences and demotion. Close relationships can drift toward a similar scorekeeping, where mistakes trigger penalties and status loss. Naming that pattern early, before it hardens, gives both people a chance to choose cooperation over punishment.

previous_copy.sections.pattern.0: When the French revolutionary government proclaimed abolition in mid-1794, Louverture changed sides, joining the French while his Spanish comrades Biassou and Papillon stayed loyal to Spain. The choice marked a public disagreement with allies he had fought beside. In everyday terms, it is the moment a person tells their own side where they differ and stands by the reason, even when the timing is awkward. That is a stance about a principle, not a template for how to treat a partner.
previous_copy.sections.pattern.2: His cultivation regulations at Port-Républicain required managers, drivers and cultivators to perform their duties under threat of arrest and punishment, with negligent drivers reduced to simple cultivators. The rules tied compliance to consequences and demotion. Close relationships can drift toward a similar scorekeeping, where mistakes trigger penalties and status loss. Naming that pattern early, before it hardens, gives both people a chance to choose cooperation over punishment.
